hints.content:
Let's find the constant  of proportionality.   

In the proportional relationship between $j$, the amount of lemon juice in $\text{mL}$, and $s$, the amount of sugar in $\text{g}$, one constant of proportionality is $\text{g}$ of sugar per $\text{mL}$ of lemon juice. It is also number we multiply by the amount of lemon juice to get the amount of sugar.

$j \,\times\, ?=s$

Lemon juice ($\text{mL}$) | Sugar ($\text{g}$) | Relationship
:-: | :-: | :-:
$500$ | $200$ |  $500\times\blueD{\dfrac{2}{5}}=200$
$750$ | $300$ | $750\times\blueD{\dfrac{2}{5}}=300$
$1500$ | $500$| $1500\times\blueD{\dfrac{2}{5}}=500$

The constant of proportionality is $\blueD{\dfrac{2}{5}}$.  This means we can multiply $\blueD{\dfrac{2}{5}}$ by the amount of lemon juice to get the amount of sugar.

Now, let's represent that as an equation.  

$\begin{align}
\text{amount of sugar}&=\blueD{\text{constant of proportionality}}\times\text{amount of juice} \\\\
s&=\blueD{\dfrac{2}{5}}j
\end{align}$

question.content:
The table below shows the amount of lemon juice and sugar needed to make three different-sized batches of lemonade using the same recipe.

| Lemon juice ($\text{mL}$) | Sugar ($\text{g}$) 
- | :-: | :-: |
Batch A | $500$ | $200$ 
Batch B | $750$ | $300$
Batch C | $1500$ | $600$

**Write an equation to describe the relationship between $j$, the amount of lemon juice in milliliters, and $s$, the amount of sugar in grams.**  
*Equations may include exact decimals,  proper fractions, or improper fractions. Please do NOT round or use mixed numbers.*
